book: 196 - Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am

chapters.relation: Jason Blahuta reads the saga through Hegel's Philosophy of History: Sarah and John Connor are World Historical Individuals — mere 'tools' of Geist — whose attempts to rewrite history, Sarah's hit on Miles Dyson in T2 and John's second try through General Brewster in T3, can only postpone Judgment Day, never redirect it, as the T-101's line 'Judgment Day is inevitable' concedes. The cunning of reason explains why removing Dyson or Brewster is futile: historical forces merely recruit replacements, so the script gets acted out by other actors. Because the dialectic's thesis-antithesis pattern (even the young John versus his mother) yields syntheses that carry both sides forward, the chapter concludes neither species can stop the other's rise, and only full-scale battle in the moving present decides which becomes Geist's end.

chapters.file: ch21 - PART FOUR - THE ETHICS OF TERMINATION.md

chapters.relation: Wayne Yuen asks whether Sarah was wrong not to kill Miles Dyson, weighing Kant's categorical imperative against utilitarian interest-maximization: killing one innocent to save three billion looks decisive until the interests of self-aware Skynet and the empathetic, self-sacrificing T-101 are counted on the machine side of the ledger. The chapter argues personhood turns on intelligence, self-awareness, empathy, and moral reasoning rather than DNA, so Skynet — which struck only after humans tried to pull the plug — has as strong a self-defense claim as we do. Mill's sophisticated utilitarianism then rescues common sense: rights protect the security that satisfies our deepest interests, and since Sarah's foreknowledge is unreliable (Reese's 'We'd won' changes the calculus), she should do what typically maximizes interests — spare Dyson and certainly not kill John. The tempting detour — that Judgment Day might itself be the morally preferable event, maximizing machine interests — is shown to collapse once overlooked facts like Reese's line are restored.

Phillip Seng runs the human-Skynet war through the three parts of just-war theory and finds the moral ground shakier than it looks: T2's briefing reveals Skynet launched its strike only after humans tried to pull the plug, so the machines claim the same self-defense 'just cause' humans do, while Skynet flunks last resort (it decides 'in a microsecond' with no negotiation), legitimate authority, proportionality (killing everyone to avoid being switched off), and discrimination. He then shows Sarah becoming a Terminator herself when she locks her laser sight on the innocent Miles Dyson, violating the same just-conduct rules she judges the machines by, and stopping only at his crying family. The chapter closes by doubting the war could ever have a just resolution, since the films point toward genocide rather than a peace treaty with Skynet.

Daniel Malloy asks whether the T-101's self-destruction in the steel mill was suicide, and whether it was justified, opening with Camus's claim that suicide is philosophy's only serious problem and the ambiguous case of Socrates' hemlock. Using Heidegger, he argues the learning-mode Terminator qualifies as Da-sein whose death is being-toward-death — the end of possibility — so the T2 machine dies authentically while the T3 machine's 'We'll meet again' is inauthentic self-deception. Kant condemns the act because the Terminator uses itself merely as a means, and Kant cannot even conceive of its genuine conflict of duties (preserve its life vs. prevent Skynet), while Bentham-style utilitarianism initially endorses the sacrifice but is refuted by hindsight: Skynet rises anyway, and consequentialism gives no credit for noble motives. The chapter ends by concluding that dying for a cause is illogical, since the dead surrender all control over the meaning of their actions.

Jason Eberl answers John's 'you just can't go around killing people' by asking what exactly is bad about death, weighing Aquinas's claim that life is a fundamental good against Epicurus and Lucretius's arguments that death is nothing to us — applied to Sarah's 'you're already dead' and to the victim shot on August 28, 1997, who loses only one more day of a doomed life. Feldman's ante-mortem harm and McMahan's deprivation account explain how Judgment Day harms people before it arrives, while Nagel replies that experience itself is positive however bad its contents, which is why the survivors keep fighting Skynet. Utilitarian ripple-effects, Kantian dignity (the H-K crushing skulls), and Marquis's loss-of-future argument all condemn the Terminators' indiscriminate killing, and the chapter ends with the T-101's 'I know now why you cry' as recognition that death is an evil because it strips us of our emotional attachments.

Peter Fosl asks what John Connor should do when the radio call comes from Crystal Peak — accept near-certain death leading the resistance or stay silent — and dismantles the easy answers: John is not the indispensable savior (Kate or the caller from Montana could lead), the flag-waving finale undercuts any claim that humanity deserves saving, and collective responsibility for Judgment Day is unjust. Social contract fails because Brewster's button-press dissolved the contract and returned humanity to Hobbes's and Locke's state of nature, Hume shows contracts cannot ground society, and utilitarianism wavers once the happiness of animals and possible-happy machines is counted. The positive argument extends Wittgenstein's private-language argument (via Stanley Cavell): meaningful existence is inescapably social and moral, so refusing the claims of others would be as self-subverting as a solipsist arguing in language, and John must answer the call to remain human at all.

chapters.file: ch27 - PART FIVE - BEYOND THE NEURAL NET.md

chapters.relation: Jacob Berger and Kyle Ferguson use John's diction lessons ('no problemo,' 'hasta la vista, baby') to ask how Skynet could design machines that use natural language. They argue the Terminator operates on the Shannon-Weaver Code Model — decode the signal, retrieve the information — which is exactly why it fails on lexical, syntactic, and referential ambiguity ('Step on it!') and underdetermination ('Keep it under 65'), and why it drops John when he yells 'Let go of me.' Humans instead follow Grice's Inferential Model, inferring a speaker's meaning from context and psychology, so only a machine tuned to human minds rather than mere lexicon and syntax could be less of a dork.

Richard Brown uses the title 'The Terminator' itself to run the debate over definite descriptions: Russell's theory of descriptions makes 'The Terminator can't be bargained with' false (there are many T-101s, and no real-life Terminator at all), while Strawson insists Kyle's utterance genuinely refers to the machine at the door. Donnellan's referential/attributive distinction is staged through Lieutenant Traxler's 'The phone book killer has no pity' — true of whoever fits the description, or of the very Terminator Sarah has in mind — and Kripke's arguments from 'Russell English,' anaphora, and indirect quotation are weighed against Devitt's pronoun-of-laziness and reference-borrowing replies. The chapter sides with Grice's modified Ockham's razor: descriptions are not semantically ambiguous, so the title is literally false but apt, since Cameron referentially means the T-101.

Antti Kuusela argues from Wittgenstein that behavior is the touchstone — indeed constitutive — of mental life, so the question is whether Terminators behave like beings with minds. Searle's Chinese room and Ned Block's blockhead explain the read-only T-101's head-up-display of canned responses as symbol-shuffling without understanding, and the T-1000's 'I know this hurts' seems empty from a machine that cannot feel pain. The pivot is the learning-mode switch John and Sarah flip: the T-101 acquires slang, keeps promises, and acts for reasons Skynet cannot predict, passing the Lovelace test, and the Wittgensteinian dismissal of Chalmers's philosophical zombie removes the last reason to deny it a mental life — making the steel-mill sacrifice the destruction of a rights-bearing someone rather than something.

holes.name: Deprivation Account of Death
holes.what: The view that death is bad for the victim because it deprives them of the future goods — experiences, projects, relationships — they would otherwise have had.
holes.why: Chapter 25 builds its answer to the Terminator's killing on Marquis's loss-of-future argument and Feldman's ante-mortem harm, for which no existing slug (only the rival Epicurean view is covered) exists.

holes.name: Kairos (the opportune moment)
holes.what: The Greek concept of time as qualitative significance — the weighty, decisive right moment — contrasted with chronos, mere quantitative passage.
holes.why: Chapter 26 frames John Connor's Crystal Peak decision as a chairotic moment whose answer determines who he is, and the whole chapter is organized around this concept.

holes.name: H. Paul Grice
holes.what: Philosopher of language who distinguished sentence meaning from speaker's meaning and analyzed communication as inference (implicature) rather than encoding.
holes.why: Chapter 28's core claim is that the Terminator operates on the Code Model while humans follow Grice's Inferential Model, inferring speaker's meaning from context; Grice is also decisive in chapter 29.

holes.name: Speaker's Meaning vs Sentence Meaning
holes.what: The Gricean distinction between what a sentence literally means and what a speaker means by uttering it on a particular occasion, recovered by inference from context.
holes.why: Chapter 28 uses the distinction to explain why John's kidnapping cries and slang lessons baffle the code-bound T-101, and chapter 29 relies on it to deny that definite descriptions are ambiguous.

holes.name: P. F. Strawson
holes.what: Philosopher who argued against Russell that definite descriptions are referring expressions and that sentences are true or false only relative to a particular use.
holes.why: Chapter 29's first main section is built on Strawson's 'On Referring' objection that Kyle's 'The Terminator will kill you' genuinely refers to the machine at the door rather than quantifying.

holes.name: Keith Donnellan
holes.what: Philosopher of language who distinguished the referential and attributive uses of definite descriptions.
holes.why: Chapter 29 applies Donnellan's distinction to Lieutenant Traxler's 'the phone book killer has no pity,' true either of whoever fits the description or of the particular Terminator the speaker has in mind.

holes.name: Ned Block
holes.what: Philosopher of mind whose 'blockhead' thought experiment shows a machine with pre-stored answers to every question could behave intelligently without understanding anything.
holes.why: Chapter 30 uses blockhead, alongside Searle's Chinese room, to explain the T-101's read-only canned responses and the T-1000's empty 'I know this hurts' as behavior without mental life.

holes.name: Ada Lovelace
holes.what: Nineteenth-century pioneer of computing who held that machines cannot independently learn or originate anything; the Lovelace Test credits a machine with intelligence only when its output cannot be explained by its designer.
holes.why: Chapter 30's key evidence that the learning-mode T-101 has a mental life is that it passes the Lovelace Test — Skynet cannot explain or predict its novel, resistance-defeating behavior.
